newsitem.title: SRI LANKA: Sri Lanka cracking down on child sex abuse.
newsitem.headline: Sri Lanka cracking down on child sex abuse.

text.p: Sri Lanka, cracking down on child sexual abuse, is taking three foreigners to court this week, police and children's rights activists said on Wednesday.

One of them, a Swiss businessman, was brought before a magistrate near the resort town of Negombo, 38 km (24 miles) north of Colombo, on Wednesday and released on bail after his passport was impounded, police said.
The businessman was arrested two weeks ago while he was in the company of three boys aged between 11 and 16, said Noel Francis, assistant superintendent at the police crimes division.
The man, a resident in Sri Lanka, was not engaged in sexual acts at the time, Francis added.
The boys first claimed they visited the man to learn English but later confessed to having sex with him, he said.
Police said the court had not charged the man yet. He is to appear in court again at a later date.

"This is one of the wealthiest men on whom charges of child sexual abuse have been brought," said Maureen Seneviratne of Protecting Environment and Children Everywhere (PEACE), a group trying to curb child sex tourism.
Cases against two other foreigners, Swiss Armin Pfaffhauser and Belgian Luc Coomans, come up in separate courts this week, police said.
Pfaffhauser and Coomans have been charged with having committed an act of gross indecency with children. Both have pleaded not guilty, they said.
Last year, Sri Lanka passed tough new laws aimed at discouraging foreign tourists seeking sex with children and put police on alert for paedophiles.

The law calls for a minimum five years in jail and a maximum 20-year sentence for pimps and their clients. It raised the minimum age of consent to 18 for boys and 16 for girls, making sex with anyone under those ages a crime.
"Now courts can give enhanced punishments to those guilty of paedophilia," said Kalyananda Tiranagama of Lawyers for Human Rights and Development, a non-governmental organisation.
"This should be a deterrent to those who abuse our children, but it alone is not enough," Tiranagama said.

Last week police launched a probe of a Belgian tour operator suspected of setting up an orphanage as a front for a child-sex ring, a practice paedophiles have increasingly turned to skirt the law, activists said.
Human rights groups have said Sri Lanka, which relies on tourism as a main source of foreign exchange and employment, has become a popular destination for paedophiles.

"We are for tourism, but we're not for making this country a sex paradise," said Anthony Pinto, a Catholic priest who runs the Don Bosco Technical Centre for sexually abused children in Negombo. He said an estimated 20,000 children in Sri Lanka are being abused by paedophiles.
"People come and spoil our kids. If they cannot come to our country, our kids would be much better off," Pinto said.

Tiranagama said activists were lobbying the government to take a tougher stand on allowing bail to suspected paedophiles, and to impress upon courts to be more sympathetic towards the children to make their court experience less traumatic.
"There is some improvement in the law. Certainly more people are concerned and the general awareness on paedophilia is high. We're heading in the right direction," he said.
